sourceDesc.p: Traduction anglaise originale produite avec l'assistance d'un modele de langage (Claude, Anthropic), a partir du texte grec de zoo71/3g.xml (edition Sbordone 1936, "Redactio tertia quae vocatur pseudo-Basiliana", pp. 259-299), lui-meme deja present dans le corpus Zoomathia. Traduction generee par IA, non relue par un specialiste : a verifier avant tout usage scientifique cite. 30 chapitres correspondant exactement au decoupage du temoin grec (memes xml:id).

div.head: Concerning the Lion
div.p: The lion has three natures.

Concerning which Jacob made mention in his prophecy: "Judah is a lion's whelp; from the shoot, my son, you have gone up; you crouched down, you slept as a lion and as a lion's whelp -- who shall rouse him?"

The first nature of the lion: when the lioness is about to give birth to her cub, she bears it dead, and the cub lies so for three days; then the lion, its father, comes, licks it over and warms it, and thus the cub rises up.

Interpretation of Saint Basil. The great Basil gave this an allegorical, spiritual interpretation, adapting the natures of the irrational animals set down by the most wise Solomon. He said: where are those who disbelieve in the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ? If the lion has the power to raise up his own cub, how did the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ not have the power to raise up His own Son? So God, coming after the crucifixion, raised up that very Son begotten of Him before the ages without flux, and in these last times from the Virgin without seed. For of Him Jacob said: "Judah's lion's whelp, from the shoot, my son, you have gone up," because from a shoot and from the tribe of Judah our Lord Jesus Christ sprang forth according to the flesh.
Second nature of the lion. Concerning which David made mention in the Psalms, saying: "O Lord, seize not my soul like a lion, while there is none to redeem or to save."

The Physiologus said that the lion, finding nothing to eat, going about in a desert field or on a mountain, circles round and marks out a wide space with his tail, dragging it along the ground as if making a fold; and when he comes back near where he began, he lies stretched out on the ground with his eyes open. Then the small animals, waking and terrified at the lion's passing, huddle together seeking a way out where the lion did not go -- and finding none, they draw near even to the lion, wishing to pass through; then the lion rises up, seizes them, and devours them.

Saint Basil, interpreting, said: see then, you too, O man, as you run and wander about in this transient life -- abide in the will of God, lest you fall into the snares of the lion, that is, of the devil; for he, even though invisible to men, presses in temptations to swallow up whomever he may, as a lion within his own fold.

The third nature of the lion: when the lion is hunted, he covers the tracks of his feet, dragging his tail over the ground; and the hunters, coming and not finding the tracks, turn back having accomplished nothing.

Saint Basil, interpreting, said: see, you too, O man, how the beast contrives to work out his own safety. You, being a rational being, cover your rear parts -- that is, your sins -- through repentance, fleeing and running to the Church and to the spiritual Fathers, so that when the hunters -- that is, the demons -- come and find no track of sin in you, they may turn back having accomplished nothing.

div.head: Concerning the Unicorn
div.p: Concerning which David made mention in the Psalms: "and my only-begotten from the horns of the unicorns."

The Physiologus spoke concerning the unicorn: the first nature of the unicorn is this -- it is a swift-running beast, having one horn, and it bears a grudge against men; pursuing a man, if it overtakes him, it saws him through the middle with its horn and eats him.

Saint Basil says: see then, you too, O man, and guard yourself against the unicorn, that is, against the demon. For he bears a grudge against men and is skilled in doing evil, and by night and by day he runs and saws at man through evil thoughts, separating him from the commandments of God.

The second nature of the unicorn: when hunters go into the woods, they watch where the elephant beds down, and having found it they saw through the tree, leaving a little of it uncut. Then the elephant, coming as usual, wishing to rest against it -- for it has no joints allowing it to bend its knees to the ground, but leans upon the tree -- being of enormous size, falls down together with the tree. Falling to the ground, the elephant cries out greatly. The hunters, having anticipated this, cut it up and carry off the flesh with the bones and flee, lest the unicorn come upon them and they become its food. But if the unicorn, hearing the elephant's voice, arrives first, it raises the elephant up, bending its own knees, and thrusting its horn into the middle of the elephant, lifts it up.

Saint Basil said: the unicorn is figuratively understood as the Lord. For our Lord Jesus Christ is interpreted as "the horn of salvation"; seeing man fallen and being moved with compassion, He came and raised him up as king of all. And if one of the hearers should say: why do you liken the Lord to wild beasts? For the Lord Himself said in the Gospels: "beware of false prophets, for they come to you in sheep's clothing, but inwardly they are ravenous wolves" -- to this you might answer: these things are understood figuratively; it is not that beasts are transformed, but that there are, among beasts, dispositions naturally good and evil: the good dispositions are likened also to Christ and to His saints, the evil ones to demons and to wicked men.

div.head: Concerning the Wolf
div.p: The first nature of the wolf. Concerning which our Lord Jesus Christ made mention in the Gospels: "beware of false prophets, for they come to you in sheep's clothing, but inwardly are ravenous wolves."

The Physiologus spoke concerning the wolf, that it is a deceitful and wicked animal; for coming to snatch from the flock of sheep, it holds its mouth open, and having seized its prey, flees because of the shepherd.

The great Basil said: such are the heretics, going about in sheep's clothing, while their hearts are like ravenous wolves, seizing the simpler folk and destroying their souls. Such also are the greedy, many men who defraud the poor -- the rich man snatching from him his field or his vineyard or something else of his possessions, unafraid of the fear of God.
The second nature of the wolf: when it meets some man, it makes itself appear lame, having no wound at all in its foot; yet its heart is full of guile and rapacity.

Saint Basil said: such also are deceitful and treacherous men; when they meet certain good men, they make themselves appear attentive, as in innocence, possessing nothing wicked -- yet their heart is full of bitterness and guile.

div.head: Concerning the Stag
div.p: The first nature of the stag. Concerning which David made mention in the Psalms: "as the hart longs for the springs of water, so my soul longs for you, O God."

The Physiologus spoke concerning it, that the stag eats the serpent and seeks a spring of water to drink, so as to dissolve the serpent's venom, and after drinking, the venom of the serpent ceases from it.

And you too, O man, seek and long for the true spring, that is, our Lord Jesus Christ, that the venom of the serpent -- that is, wickedness and the demon's temptation -- may flee from you, and you may find rest of body and of soul.

The second nature of the stag. The Physiologus spoke concerning it, that when the hunters pursue it, it goes up into the mountains and mingles with other stags, and mixing among them it escapes their notice, and so is saved.

Saint Basil says: the stag works out its own salvation; you too, being a rational being, O man, run to the mountains, that is, to spiritual men, mingle with them in virtue and manner of life, and when the hunters -- that is, the demons -- come, they will turn back having accomplished nothing.

div.head: Concerning the Panther
div.p: There is an animal called the panther. The Physiologus spoke concerning it, that it is exceedingly beautiful and loving toward all the beasts; for as it sleeps, a sweet fragrance goes forth from its mouth, and as if drawn by that fragrance all the beasts encircle it, leaping around the panther, and rejoice, and after each of them has rejoiced, they depart glad and exulting into the woods and fields.

Saint Basil said: the panther takes on the person and image of our Lord Jesus Christ; for our Lord Jesus Christ, coming from the Father and appearing in the world as a man, from His teaching a sweet fragrance went forth from His mouth, and all the nations came to know the Holy Trinity, and drawn by the fragrance of His mouth the prophets and the apostles and the martyrs ran to Him, and the whole choir of the saints, and rejoicing they went forth into the eternal tabernacles.

div.head: Concerning the Beaver
div.p: There is an animal called the beaver. The Physiologus spoke concerning it: when the hunters pursue it, knowing that it is pursued for the sake of its genitals, it bites them off and leaves them on the ground; and the hunters, coming and finding its organs, turn back having accomplished nothing, and thus the beaver is saved.

Saint Basil said: this animal, knowing whence harm comes to it, casts away the harm and goes off saved; and you, being a rational being, O man, how do you remain in carelessness? Have you not heard the Lord saying: "if your eye or your hand causes you to stumble, cut it off from you"? He did not say this concerning the members of the body, but concerning kinsmen and friends and brothers: if you have among your kinsmen and friends and brothers any who harm you in soul, cut them off from you as the beaver does its organs, and when your mind becomes free of care, then you will have leisure for God and find grace.

div.head: Concerning the Fox
div.p: Concerning which David made mention in the Psalms, saying: "they shall be a portion for foxes."

The Physiologus spoke concerning it: the fox is a deceitful animal. When it is hungry, it goes to a dunghill place and lies on its back, holding its breath, and puffs itself up entirely; and the birds, seeing it, come down upon it to eat it, thinking it is dead; but it, seizing them, eats of the birds. And again, this fox, finding the hare, lures it by playing with it, and having seized it, eats it.

Saint Basil said: in the portion of foxes shall be the envious and the mockers and thieves, because whether lying down or rising up they appear to men gentle and tame, but in their heart, in their wickedness and evil disposition, they scheme within what they may seize from their neighbor, having no sense of the fear of God, nor keeping it in their hearts.

div.head: Concerning the Crocodile
div.p: The Physiologus spoke concerning the crocodile, that it is an aquatic animal, found in rivers and in lakes; in front, down to the navel, it appears like a lion, and from the navel downward like a serpent; when it seizes some man, it eats him from the feet up to the neck vertebra; and when it comes near the head, it sits down lamenting over him.

Of such a disposition are found, says Saint Basil, many of those in high positions -- the greedy and the unjust, who devour the poor; but coming to the head, that is, before the judge, our Lord Jesus Christ I mean (for Christ is the head of all), when they stand before the righteous judge, they will weep and lament for themselves because of their wicked deeds, but to no avail; for there is no repentance in Hades, nor any pleading before the righteous judge. But you, if you wish to be shown mercy, show mercy to him whom you wrong, and do not become like the crocodile, lest you hear from the judge: "you showed no mercy, you shall receive none."

div.head: Concerning the Serpent
div.p: Concerning which the Lord said in the Gospels: "be therefore as wise as serpents."

The Physiologus spoke concerning the serpent, that it has four natures. The first nature is this: when a man is about to kill it, it gives up its whole body to death, but guards its head so that it may not be struck.

Saint Basil says: so you too, O man, when someone afflicts you for Christ's sake, guard your head, keeping the faith of Christ unshaken, so that you may show yourself wise as a serpent in Christ. And how did the Lord call wise the serpent which He cursed? Listen: the curse, on account of the transgression, fell both upon the devil and upon the serpent, but the Lord did not praise it for its wickedness, but for the guarding of its head. For this He said: "be wise as serpents" -- that is, be as wise as the serpent, and guard your head, that is, the faith of Christ.
The second nature of the serpent: when the serpent goes to a spring to drink water, it leaves its venom in its lair, and thus goes to drink water.

Saint Basil says: and you too, O man, when you go to drink from the true spring -- that is, the body and blood of Christ -- do not bring wickedness into your heart, according to the Apostle; if you go into the Church and there remember that someone has something against you, go first and be reconciled with your brother, and then offer your gift. He who unworthily eats and drinks the body and blood of the Lord, eats and drinks judgment upon himself, not discerning the body and blood of the Lord.

The third nature of the serpent: when the serpent grows old, its eyes grow dim, and then it enters into its lair and fasts forty days, and constrains its body through self-restraint; its skin grows loose, and then it seeks the cracks of a rock or a narrow place, and squeezing itself, it sheds its skin and is renewed.

Saint Basil said: see, O man, how the serpent conducts its own salvation; fast, then, you too, so that through self-restraint you may be renewed and come into the will of God. Fasting was ordained in paradise: the first commandment which Adam received, had he kept it, he would not have been condemned to death. Cast off, then, the old man, that is, your sins, and seek the crack of the rock or narrow place as the serpent does; for narrow and constricted is the way that leads to eternal life, but broad and spacious the way that leads to destruction.

The fourth nature of the serpent: when the serpent finds a man clothed in garments, it leaps upon him; but if it sees him naked, it flees in terror, knowing that the fall into nakedness came about through it and was its cause; so, ashamed, it flees.

Saint Basil says: the serpent understood spiritually is the demon; when he sees you clothed in evil habits, he leaps upon you, and forces you to do the works of darkness; but when he sees you stripped bare of foul deeds and of the cares of this life, then, ashamed, he flees from you.

div.head: Concerning the Viper
div.p: Saint John the Forerunner said to the Jews: "you brood of vipers, who warned you to flee from the wrath to come?"

The Physiologus spoke concerning it: when the viper is about to give birth, it climbs up onto a tree and so gives birth without fear; but if it gives birth on the ground, its offspring devour the father and the mother.

Saint Basil says that the Forerunner, seeing the wickedness and the unforgiving disposition of the Jews, called them slayers of their father and mother, because they killed their prophets and their forefathers, who proclaimed their salvation and taught them concerning the kingdom of heaven; they showed no mercy to those they had forgotten, but killed one and stoned another, as the viper does.

div.head: Concerning the Asp
div.p: Concerning which David made mention: "like a deaf asp that stops her ears, which will not listen to the voice of charmers; she is charmed cunningly by a skilled one."

The Physiologus spoke concerning it, that when it lies down, it places one ear upon the ground, and with the other, raising its tail, covers it, so as not to hear the incantation of the skilled charmer. When, then, one who knows its trick wishes to hunt it, he goes and smears himself with cattle dung, and draws near to it; and it, as though longing for the dung of cattle, uncovers its tail; and the skilled man, chanting his incantation over it, the asp is no longer able to move at all, but is at once rendered as if dead; he then goes at once and cuts it to pieces, and departs as a victor.

Saint Basil said: just as the asp stops her ears, so too the devil, seeing our Lord Jesus Christ wearing our flesh -- for he hid his divinity as one wise, and going down into Hades, revealed his divinity there, having power over both the living and the dead. The devil, hearing his voice, was rendered as if dead, like the asp; and He, having raised up man, granted us life eternal; wherefore it was said: "she is charmed cunningly by a skilled one."

div.head: Concerning the Wild Boar
div.p: Concerning which David made mention: "and the wild boar out of the wood has ravaged it," that is, my vineyard.

The Physiologus spoke concerning it: it comes out of the woodland into the open, seeking water in which to wallow, and then, made bold, it goes off into the vineyard, devouring the clusters, and biting and chewing lays it waste; but if it finds the vineyard fenced, it cannot enter it, nor can it get at what hangs high.

Saint Basil said: "the boar out of the wood" David likens to the devil, and "the vineyard" to the world. The devil, having gone forth from the will of God, goes about watching for an unguarded soul that has no fear of God, and finding one, enters and devours it through shameful thoughts, and wallows it in the mire of sin; but if he finds a soul fenced about in the will of God, he withdraws and flees from it, unable to plunder the house of the soul. The Lord too is interpreted as the vine; for He said to His disciples: "I am the vine, you are the branches." So the man who remains in the will of God, keeping his mind lifted up like the branch hanging on its supports -- the devil, never satisfied, always warring against men, finding no way to govern the righteous through carelessness, since they remain in the will of God, flees from them; but if he finds some man living carelessly, entering in, he lays waste the house of his soul, and thus the man perishes.

div.head: Concerning the Ant
div.p: Solomon in his Proverbs said: "go to the ant, O sluggard"; for he, discoursing on the natures of the irrational and creeping animals, said that the ant has three natures.

Its first nature is this: when it goes about at harvest, each one carrying its own burden departs, and meeting one another they greet each other affectionately, and the one not carrying a grain does not envy his neighbor, but himself runs and seeks his own burden.

Saint Basil said: imitating, O man, the ant as it goes, and seeing those who strive for the Lord's sake, bearing their own virtues as spiritual burdens -- for going about at harvest, that is, in this transient life, gathering, they lay them up in storehouses, that is, in the treasuries of God, so that when the winter of this transient life overtakes them, they may find rest for their labor, according to the word of the Lord: "come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest" -- so you too, O man, imitating the lives of the saints, will find rest in the hour of winter; and do not wish to seize what belongs to your neighbor, lest you be condemned as the slothful servant who took the talent and hid it in the earth.

The second nature of the ant: when the first rains come, what does the ant do? Taking out the seeds, that is, the grains of wheat, it cuts them through the middle, and so stores them away, fearing lest through the rain and the richness of the earth they take root, and it, having nothing to eat, should perish.

Saint Basil said: see then, you too, O man, and pluck out the evil habits from your heart, lest, as when rains come, the demon's thoughts take root in your heart, and you perish in a famine of good works, possessing no good habits; but cut off from yourself fornication, adultery, theft, idle talk, abuse, drunkenness, strife, envy, wrath, love of novelty, slander, love of money -- the second idolatry -- and all forbidden things; for so the Psalmist also teaches: "turn from evil and do good, and you shall find rest."

The third nature of the ant: when the ant goes to gather grains from the ears of corn, it smells at the root, and by the smell it knows whether it is barley or wheat; and if it is wheat, it climbs up the ears and carries down the grain, but if it is barley, it does not climb up, knowing that it is food for irrational animals.

Saint Basil said: the ant, gathering the good, avoids the shameful; and you, being a rational being, O man, why do you prefer shameful deeds above good ones? Know that sin is the food of irrational creatures, in which the devil delights, but wheat is the food of men, and all the righteous have eaten of it. Wheat and bread is our Lord Jesus Christ; for He commanded, saying: "I am the bread that came down from heaven." Seeking this bread, the saints have eaten it, and live forever.

div.head: Concerning Frogs
div.p: The Physiologus spoke concerning them, that there are frogs of the water and frogs of the dry land; the land-frogs, when winter overtakes them, unable to bear the frost and the rains, perish; the water-frogs, when the sun's burning heat overtakes them, having no water, likewise also perish.

Saint Basil said: such are many of the half-hearted and of monks; when some temptation overtakes them, they cannot bear it, and even being monks, they are troubled by their thoughts, saying: "in this monastery we have no rest; our superior pays us no heed; the brothers despise us; the rule is too strict in this monastery -- let us go away to another monastery, that we may govern others, and not others govern us." And after leaving the monastery, Satan receives them, casting evil thoughts into them, and moving them from monastery to monastery, from house to house, he does not let them find rest, nor to live in quiet. But the man who is rational and fears God devotes himself unceasingly to God, enduring the temptations that come upon him. Many, being tempted and enduring, shall receive a greater reward, as did the blessed Job; but the faint of heart, not enduring, perish like the frogs.

div.head: Concerning the Eagle
div.p: Concerning which Moses made mention: "as an eagle that shelters its nest, and yearns over its young."
The Physiologus spoke concerning the eagle, that it has two natures.

Its first nature is this: when the eagle makes its nest, it shelters it and watches over its young; and when the male goes forth, the female guards them, and again when the female goes forth for food, the male guards them, and it does not let any beast, nor creeping thing, nor any other bird come near its nest, but keeps it in safety.

Saint Basil said: the nest is interpreted as the world; our Lord Jesus Christ, looking upon the world and upon His young, that is, upon mankind, and being moved with compassion, came down to His nest, guarding us from the deceit of idols and from the blood-thirsty Jews who slew the prophets, driving out every creeping thing, and keeping us in the orthodox faith, that we might keep and always guard His commandments, and holding us in the Church as in a nest, in His keeping. "Do not let your foot be moved, and He who keeps you will not slumber."
The second nature of the eagle. Concerning which David made mention: "your youth shall be renewed like the eagle's."
The Physiologus spoke concerning it: when the eagle grows old, it seeks out a spring and plunges into it three times, and is renewed, casting off its aged feathers.

Saint Basil said: the eagle, knowing what is good, seeks its own renewal, though it is but a bird; and you, being a rational being, why do you not seek the renewal of your soul? Seek then the immortal spring, our Lord Jesus Christ, being baptized through the washing of regeneration; and if sin has grown old within you, renew your soul through repentance; do not tarry long in sin, but strip off the old man, the mind of the flesh, which cannot be subject to the law of God; but as the eagle, so you too seek the spring, and you shall find in it eternal life.

div.head: Concerning the Dove
div.p: Concerning which the Lord made mention in the Gospels: "and harmless as doves."
The Physiologus spoke concerning it: the dove, when its master takes away her young, does not resent it nor bear a grudge, but strives to make another nest and other young in his house.

Saint Basil said: see then, O man, the word of the Lord, and imitate the dove; for the Lord did not say that you should become a bird, nor change your nature, but that you should have the disposition of bearing no grudge. If someone takes from you your cloak or something of yours, out of love for Christ, give up to him the other also; for He promised His disciples, saying: "blessed are you when they reproach you and persecute you for my sake, and say all manner of evil against you falsely."

div.head: Concerning the Turtledove
div.p: The Physiologus spoke concerning it, that the turtledove is faithful to its mate for its whole life, and if the male is hunted down, from then on she does not join with other turtledoves, but goes about grieving, seeking her companion; and she perches neither on a green tree, but sitting on a dry one, mourning, she keeps to her single union.

Saint Basil said: imitate then, O women, the turtledove, and keep the marriage-bed of your husband as the turtledove does, according to the apostle Paul: "marriage is honorable, and the bed undefiled." Not only women, but all persons -- for God will judge fornicators and adulterers; keep then your virtues, that God may receive you into the eternal tabernacles as undefiled; for blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.

div.head: Concerning the Hoopoe
div.p: There is a bird called the hoopoe. The Physiologus spoke concerning it, that when its parents grow old, listen to what the young birds do: the children, flying together, make a nest and set their parents, now dim of sight, within it; and one of them sits warming the parents, while the other provides food, and thus they continue until the parents cast off their aged feathers, and are so renewed, and they go about together rejoicing.

Saint Basil said: you, being a rational being, O man, care for your parents in their old age, imitating the bird, so that you may have their blessing also, and find grace with Christ; for He said: "whoever does not honor father or mother shall die the death." What benefit is it for a man to see his parents in weakness and not help them, but rather give to others and disregard his parents? If anyone says, "I love Christ," and hates his brother, he is a liar and deceives himself; if you hate your brother whom you have seen, how can you love Christ whom you have not seen? As for the Lord's saying: "whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me" -- He did not say this concerning hating one's parents, but concerning the word "more," that is, above me or beyond measure. It is preferable to love the Lord above all things seen, and to honor one's parents, and for every man to abide in the love of Christ -- those who believe rightly -- for God is love, and he who abides in love abides in God; but to turn away from blasphemers and to hate the unfaithful, and to imitate those who are good and serve God, and to rejoice in what is good.

div.head: Concerning the Ostrich
div.p: The Physiologus spoke concerning it, that when it is about to lay its eggs, it knows the season of the air, and when great heat comes upon the air, it goes to the shore and lays there, and after laying it covers them with sand, and goes away forgetting them; and as the eggs are warmed by the sun's heat, the little birds come forth, and they are called ostriches.

Saint Basil said: such are unmindful parents; abandoning their children, they go about in carelessness, taking no thought to nourish them. Such too are spiritual fathers, who gladly receive their spiritual children in confession, and then live carelessly, remembering their children neither in prayer nor in vigil, though begging the Lord's help for their own sins -- not knowing that they themselves must give account before the righteous judge, according to the Apostle.

div.head: Concerning the Heron
div.p: Concerning which David made mention in the Psalms, saying: "the dwelling of the heron is chief among them."

The Physiologus spoke concerning it, that the heron is a bird, and it is beloved by its young; when it makes its nest and the chicks come forth, they strike their father or mother, biting them; and the mother, in her pain, strikes them, and they die; and then the heron flies up into the air above the nest, and beats its own sides with its wings, until it bleeds and the blood drips down upon the little birds, and so they are brought back to life.

Saint Basil said: the heron takes on the image of our Lord Jesus Christ; for when He came and was made flesh, the unmindful Jews crucified Him and opened His side, and His precious blood dripped forth, and gave us life, as the Lord who loves mankind, being moved with compassion for us. For He is the Savior and Father of all, and He makes His sun to rise on the evil and the good, and sends rain on the just and the unjust; for He said: "when I am lifted up, I will draw all men to myself." He drew us from the error of idols, though we were dead in sin; for this the Psalmist said: "the dwelling of the heron is chief among them."

div.head: Concerning the Phoenix
div.p: The Physiologus spoke concerning it, that the phoenix is a bird, and its nature is this: every three years it goes into paradise and takes from the fragrant trees and spices that are in paradise, filling its wings and its feet, and goes to the temple in Egypt. And the priest, knowing the nature of the phoenix, makes for it a bed of coals upon the altar, and the phoenix enters and is burned together with the fragrant woods, until it becomes ashes, and the whole temple is filled with fragrance. And the next day the priest comes and examines the ashes, and finds within them a worm; and on the second day he finds it become like a winged fledgling; and on the third day it becomes perfect, as it was before; and the priest prays, and blessing it, it returns to its own dwelling.

Saint Basil said: where are the unmindful Jews, who disbelieve the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ? If the bird sacrifices itself and rises again, how did He who has power over both the living and the dead not rise? For the Son and Word of God, coming from the heavens, and taking flesh from the ever-virgin Mary, through the fragrances of His divinity made us divine, sacrificing that very flesh upon the cross, not His divinity; for He said: "I am able to destroy this temple, and in three days build it up," speaking of His flesh; but the foolish Jews, not understanding, thought He spoke of the temple of Solomon. He was indeed able also to do this, as God who brought all things from non-being into being -- for nothing was impossible to Him -- but rising from the dead on the third day according to the Scriptures, He ascended to His own dwellings in the heavens, whence He was never absent, having taught us to mind the things above, the angelic way of life, that we might be found worthy of His heavenly kingdom.

div.head: Concerning the Parrot
div.p: The Physiologus spoke concerning it, that there is a bird called the parrot, small as a partridge; imitating the voices of men, it too speaks likewise, and converses as a man does.

Saint Basil said: imitate, then, O man, the voices of the apostles who glorified God, and glorify Him yourself too, imitating the lives of the righteous, that you may be found worthy to attain their places full of light.
Well has the Physiologus spoken concerning the parrot.

div.head: Concerning the Pheasant
div.p: The Physiologus spoke concerning it: there is a bird called the pheasant, and after hatching its young, it goes about with them. When some man comes upon it, it offers itself as easy prey before the man, making its young scatter through the field, and thus deceives him, and goes off rejoicing, having lured the man away.

Saint Basil said: thus the enemy lures men; he induces a man to commit sin, and again coming the next day, the wicked accomplice suggests: "today for me, and tomorrow for God," while Christ says: "today, if you hear my voice." Let us then, brothers, hearken to our God, who wills the good, and not to the deceiver and cheat who schemes to destroy man; for just as the bird lures the hunter, so too the devil contrives harm to our souls.

div.head: Concerning the Hedgehog (which some call ritzos, others katzochoiros)
div.p: The Physiologus spoke concerning it, that when the hedgehog gives birth, it goes to the vineyard and climbs onto the vine-branch, and seizes the clusters, and knocks the grapes down to the ground; then coming down, it rolls itself over them; and the grapes sticking to the hedgehog's spines, it goes to its own young, and the young, coming out, eat.

Saint Basil said: imitate then, O man, the hedgehog; even though it is an unclean animal, yet it possesses a way of life marked by affection and love for its offspring. Do not be a hater of children, but raise them both in flesh and in spirit -- in the flesh, providing them daily food, and in spirit, guiding them with good words. Going into the Church of God and hearing from the true vine its clusters, that is, the words of our Lord Jesus Christ, provide for your children, that being nourished on good things they may glorify the Father who is in the heavens, and hold you in honor all the days of their life.

The second nature of the hedgehog: the Physiologus spoke concerning it, that as the hedgehog goes about, if it finds a serpent, it bites it, and the hedgehog curling itself up, the serpent, torn on the outside by the hedgehog's spines, dies, and thus it eats it.

Saint Basil said: evil is destroyed by evil; when cruel men meet one another, they do not remember the word of the Lord, "love one another," but biting and envying, they seek to put each other to death, having venom in their hearts.

div.head: Concerning the Hare
div.p: Concerning which David made mention: "the rock is a refuge for the hares."

The Physiologus spoke concerning it, that when it is hunted, it takes refuge among the rocks and in the high places, and is thus saved; but if it goes down a slope, being unable to run because its forefeet are shorter, the dog quickly overtakes it, and for this reason it seeks the heights.

Saint Basil said: seek then, you too, O man, the rock, when pursued by the wicked dog, the demon, who pursues day after day to seize the life of man. If he sees a man running downhill, minding earthly and transient things of this life, then he presses upon him all the more heavily through shameful thoughts; but if he sees him running in the will of God and seeking the true rock, our Lord Jesus Christ, and ascending the heights of virtue, he turns back like a dog, according to David: "let those who wish me evil be turned back and put to shame."

div.head: Concerning the Chalandros
div.p: The Physiologus spoke concerning it, that the chalandros is a white bird, and this is its nature: when a man is sick, they bring the chalandros over the one who is ill, and if the sickness is unto death, it turns away from him; but if it is unto life, it draws near to him and places its mouth into the mouth of the sick man, and drinks his sickness, and then flies up into the air, and being scorched by the sun's heat, casts off the whole sickness, and thus all know that the sick man has been healed.

Saint Basil said: the chalandros takes on the image of our Lord Jesus Christ; for the compassionate One, coming upon the earth and seeing us sick, turned away from the Jews as being impious, but gave us life; He Himself bore our infirmities, and having granted us healing, ascended into the heavens, whence He shall come to judge the living and the dead, He who is spotless and pure.

div.head: Concerning the Pelican
div.p: Concerning which David made mention: "I have become like a pelican of the wilderness."

The Physiologus spoke concerning it: when its young hatch and are cleared from the eggs, they strike their father's face, and their father endures it, loving his offspring as he does. Its beak is hard enough to bore through trees.

Saint Basil said: our Lord and God, Jesus Christ, came down to us, to His young, and we struck Him and spat upon Him; the ungrateful Jews dared to do this, but He endured all things bearing no grudge, willingly enduring both the spitting and the buffeting, and praying for them to God the Father, He said: "do not hold this sin against them, Father, for they know not what they do." And we, sinning daily and provoking Him, He bears no grudge, but overlooks our sins, awaiting our turning back and repentance; for He does not desire the death of the sinner so much as that he should turn and live.

div.head: Concerning the Otter
div.p: This animal, then, is like a dog, dwelling by the river, and it has enmity with the crocodile; going about along the riverbank, it watches for the crocodile sleeping. Finding it with its mouth open (such being the crocodile's nature), what does the otter do? It rolls itself in the mud, and thus enters into the crocodile's mouth, and devours all its inward parts, and kills it.

Saint Basil said: such are the rich, who even as they lie in their chamber are anxious, their throat open to devour the poor man; but the poor man watches for him, and repays him when he finds the occasion. Beware then, O rich man, lest you bear a grudge against the poor man, lest He who was anointed from our flesh come and repay you on the day of judgment, and you hear the sentence of the accursed: "depart from me, you accursed, into the outer darkness," and: "you showed no mercy, you shall receive none."

div.head: Concerning the Elephant
div.p: The Physiologus spoke concerning it, that when the male is about to mate with the female, they mate facing backward, because they have no joint allowing otherwise; and the female carries the young in her womb for one year, and when she is about to give birth, she goes into a lake and gives birth in the water, so as to float in the water, and thus comes out onto the land; but she cannot rise up again, having no joint.

Saint Basil said: the animals seek their own salvation; and you, being a rational being, O man, have conceived wealth in your womb; recognize, after a time, the wealth that is laid up for you; run to the Church, and place yourself in the waters, that is, in the bosoms of the poor, so that when you go forth from this life, you may find rest.

The second nature of the elephant: when the dragon-serpent finds it, it leaps upon it, coiling round its whole body, and searches for a vein of blood, and finding one, drinks its blood; and the elephant, trembling, falls to the ground; but the serpent, unable to disentangle itself because of the weight -- for the elephant is a creature of enormous size -- is crushed and dies, and thus both the elephant and the serpent perish together.

Saint Basil said: watch, O man, lest the serpent, finding you, overtake you and coil around your whole body, drinking from you your good judgment, and the end come upon you together with it, and you go off into perdition, and hear from the righteous judge: "depart from me, you accursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels."

div.head: Concerning the Wild Ass
div.p: The Physiologus spoke concerning it, that there is an animal called the wild ass, having with it many females, as the leader of the herd, and it is jealous of the males; when a female wild ass bears a male, the father bites off its genitals with his mouth; but many females, separating from him, give birth in thickly wooded places, and thus the males survive.

Saint Basil said: of such a nature were Pharaoh and Herod, the one jealous of Israel, the other jealous of the Lord; woe to them, for they were reckoned as wild asses and beasts of dull understanding. Not they alone, but also many men shall pay the penalty, who, castrating males and changing their nature from male to female, set themselves against the Maker of the body, imagining they do something good; many of them, in removing their organs, remove their life as well. O the folly of those who do such things! The removal of the organs is accomplished and cut away, but the desire of the flesh and of pleasure never ceases warring and constraining a man; then shall you be glorified by the Lord, when the warfare of the flesh arises in you and you hold fast to virtue and withstand the warfare -- then shall you be a eunuch for Christ's sake and be glorified by Christ the King, as the soldiers of a king, when they return bearing victory and the trophy, are then rewarded by him with benefits and honors and rejoice, and dwelling securely in rest, live in the houses of the king.
